passage: Trisha, nine, had exactly fifty rupees and a list from Amma: three packets of milk and one bread. The shopkeeper was busy, and the school bus would come in ten minutes. Milk was twelve rupees a packet. "Twelve, twenty-four, thirty-six," she muttered, then stopped using her fingers. "Three twelves is thirty-six." Bread was sixteen. Her brother Jomon tugged her sleeve. "Hurry!" "Wait. Thirty-six and sixteen is fifty-two. Two more than we have." She put one milk packet back. "Two milk and bread is forty, so ten comes back." The shopkeeper counted: forty. She pocketed the ten and ran for the bus.

qa.q: How much did one packet of milk cost?
qa.a: Twelve rupees a packet.

qa.q: Why did Trisha tell Jomon to wait?
qa.a: She wanted to be sure of her sum before paying, even with the bus coming, because she was worried they might not have enough.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Multiplying instead of counting on her fingers let her find the total fast and see she was two rupees short, so she could change the order in time.

qa.q: How might Amma see Trisha bringing home two milk packets instead of three?
qa.a: She may be surprised at first but, hearing the reason, likely appreciate that Trisha worked out the money herself.

grounding: It shows a child using multiplication, addition and subtraction under time pressure instead of counting.

passage: On a rainy afternoon in their Pune flat, Simran, ten, had one big slab of peanut chikki and three others waiting, including her little cousin Nandini, who wanted the biggest piece. "Four people, so each gets a quarter," Simran said. She broke the slab in half, then each half in half again. "See? Half of a half is a quarter." Nandini squinted. "But mine looks smaller." Simran laid the four pieces side by side and lined up the edges. They matched, near enough. "Same. It's just thinner and longer." Nandini counted. "So four quarters make the whole one?" "Exactly."

qa.q: How did Simran make four pieces?
qa.a: She broke the slab in half, then broke each half in half again.

qa.q: Why did Nandini squint and say hers looked smaller?
qa.a: She was worried she was getting less and was judging by the shape of the piece rather than the fraction.

qa.q: How could Simran help Nandini trust fractions next time?
qa.a: Keep laying pieces side by side or stacking them, so Nandini can check the equal parts herself.

qa.q: What would change if there had been three people instead of four?
qa.a: Simran would need thirds, which halving cannot make, so she would have to find another way to split the slab.

grounding: It shows a ten-year-old using halves and quarters to share fairly and explaining the idea to a younger cousin.

passage:
"Mumma, what's four times three? The book just says it."
Aparna held up an egg tray. "How many rows?"
"Three."
"How many in each row?"
Chetan touched them. "Four, four, four."
"So?"
"Four... eight... twelve! Oh, so it's just adding fours quickly."
"Exactly. What if I take away one row?"
"Then four times two. Eight." He paused. "It's taking away four."
"And if we share the twelve eggs among Nani's house, Chachi's house and ours?"
"Three houses. Twelve divided by three... four each! It's backwards times!"

qa.q: How many eggs were in each row of the tray?
qa.a: Four eggs were in each row.

qa.q: What does Chetan's "Oh" show about his thinking?
qa.a: He suddenly understood that multiplying is a quick way of adding the same number again and again. 🤔

qa.q: Why did the egg tray help more than the book?
qa.a: It let Chetan see and touch the rows, so the rule came from something real instead of a fact to memorise.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel when Chetan calls division "backwards times"?
qa.a: She is likely pleased, because he has found the link himself and put it in his own words.

grounding: It shows a child moving from counting to understanding multiplication, and its link to subtraction and division.

passage: Last year I thought maths was only counting on fingers. Then Amma made four parathas and there were six of us: me, Suraj, Amma, Appa, Paati and Thatha. Suraj said, 'Not enough!' I looked at the plate and thought, what if we cut each into halves? That made eight pieces. Six people, eight pieces. Two left over. I felt so clever. Appa asked, 'And what if Thatha wants two?' I counted again. Then only one left. Now when I see fractions in class, I think of parathas.

qa.q: How many parathas did Amma make?
qa.a: She made four parathas.

qa.q: Why did the narrator feel clever?
qa.a: They worked out by themselves that cutting each paratha into halves made eight pieces, enough for six people.

qa.q: How could a teacher use this kind of example in class?
qa.a: They could use everyday food sharing to teach fractions and division, so the ideas feel real.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt on seeing the problem solved?
qa.a: Suraj might feel relieved that everyone would eat, and perhaps a bit impressed. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a child moving from counting to understanding division and fractions through sharing food.

passage:
Tuition note by Minakshi Ma'am, for Suraj's parents
Suraj used to add 7 plus 7 plus 7 plus 7 on his fingers and lose count. This week I laid out four rows of seven beads. He looked, then said, 'It's four sevens! Twenty-eight!' He tried 4 times 6 on his own with beads and then without. Then he did 3 times 5 in his head, frowning, and got it right. He also asked if subtraction can be done in groups. 👍 I have given him some practice sheets.

qa.q: How many rows of beads did Minakshi Ma'am lay out?
qa.a: She laid out four rows of seven beads.

qa.q: What does Suraj's question about subtraction in groups suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was curious and excited, and was starting to see numbers as groups rather than only counting.

qa.q: Why were beads a good choice for teaching multiplication?
qa.a: They let Suraj see repeated groups at once, which helps him move beyond counting one by one.

qa.q: How might Suraj's parents feel after reading this note?
qa.a: They would likely feel encouraged by his progress and his curiosity.

grounding: Shows a child moving from counting to understanding multiplication as groups, in a tutor's note.

passage:
Nikita's diary, Tuesday
Today I finally got fractions! Gurleen and I had one roti to share at lunch, and Ma'am had just taught halves and quarters. I tore it into two: halves. Then Gurleen said, "What if Palak wants some?" So we tore each half again: four quarters. Gurleen ate one, I ate one, Palak ate one, and one was left. That's three quarters gone, one quarter left! Dadi laughed when I told her I ate my maths.

qa.q: Into how many pieces did they tear the roti in the end?
qa.a: Four quarters.

qa.q: How was Nikita feeling about fractions by the end of the day?
qa.a: Nikita felt excited and proud to finally understand them.

qa.q: What would you advise Nikita to try next with fractions?
qa.a: Try splitting other things at home, like a chapati or a fruit, into halves, quarters or thirds and counting what's left.

qa.q: How might Gurleen see the roti lesson?
qa.a: Gurleen probably found it fun and helpful, especially since the question about Palak led to quarters.

grounding: Shows a child moving beyond counting to understand halves and quarters by sharing a roti.

passage: In the small-town shop, Vishal, nine, was helping his uncle Yash stack eggs. "How many trays?" Yash asked. "Six." "Five eggs in each. How many eggs?" Vishal started counting one by one, then stopped. "Wait. Five, ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five, thirty. Six fives is thirty!" Yash grinned. "Now three eggs broke. How many good ones?" Vishal did it in his head, lips moving. "Thirty take away three… twenty-seven." Yash handed him a pencil stub. "Write it in the book, then. You're my accountant now." Vishal wrote 30 − 3 = 27 very neatly and underlined it twice.

qa.q: How many eggs were in each tray?
qa.a: Five eggs in each.

qa.q: What does Vishal stopping his one-by-one counting suggest?
qa.a: He realised there was a faster way and felt pleased to use what he knew about multiplying.

qa.q: How could Yash keep building Vishal's maths at the shop?
qa.a: Keep asking him real questions, like totals and what's left, so he practises multiplying and subtracting.

qa.q: How might Yash feel when Vishal answers so quickly?
qa.a: Impressed and proud of his nephew's quick thinking.

grounding: Shows a child moving from counting one by one to multiplying and subtracting in a real shop task.

passage: In a flat in Johannesburg, Lindiwe, eight, and her friend Paulo stared at a pizza cut into eight slices. "Three of us, with my little sister," said Paulo. Lindiwe frowned. "Eight can't go into three fair." She counted: "Two each is six. Two left." Paulo said, "Cut the two into three parts?" "Too small," Lindiwe said. "Two slices each, and the last two we save." She put them on a plate while Paulo held the fridge door. "Six now, two later. Tomorrow we work out the two again, when we are hungry." Paulo counted on his fingers. "Six and two is eight. That's fair."

qa.q: How many slices was the pizza cut into?
qa.a: Eight slices.

qa.q: What was Lindiwe thinking when she frowned?
qa.a: She was puzzled, realising eight couldn't be shared equally by three, and wanted to find a fair way.

qa.q: Which idea worked, and why?
qa.a: Giving two slices each and saving the last two for later, because it was simple and fair for everyone.

qa.q: How might Paulo's little sister feel about the plan?
qa.a: She might be happy to get an equal share with the older children.

grounding: Shows children using division, subtraction and halves to share a pizza fairly.

passage: Sonali Ma'am poured tamarind seeds onto each desk. "Make four groups of three." Madhav counted them into small piles, lips moving. "Now, how many altogether?" He started counting one by one again. "Wait," he said. "Three, six, nine, twelve!" He looked up. "It's four times three. It's the same thing!" Sonali Ma'am smiled. "Show me five groups of two." Madhav made them fast and said, "Ten," without counting. He sat back, grinning, and pushed his seeds into a new pattern to try six times four.

qa.q: What did Sonali Ma'am pour onto each desk?
qa.a: Tamarind seeds.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel when he said, "It's the same thing!"?
qa.a: He was excited, surprised and proud at seeing that counting groups and multiplying were connected.

qa.q: How could Sonali Ma'am build on Madhav's discovery?
qa.a: She could give him larger groups or ask him to draw arrays to link the seeds to written multiplication.

qa.q: How might a classmate still counting one by one see Madhav's quick answer?
qa.a: A classmate might feel curious or a little behind and want to know his trick.

grounding: A child moves from counting seeds one by one to understanding multiplication as groups.

passage: I'm Ishita, Hrithik's older sister. On Sunday Mummy made one big paratha and said Hrithik and I had to share it with Papa and her. Hrithik, who's nine, cut it in half, then stopped. "No, four people," he said, and cut each half again. "So each is one quarter." Then he picked up a piece and said, "If I give you my quarter, you get two quarters, that's half!" I don't know what went on in his head, but last month he got mixed up with fractions. Today he looked so sure.

qa.q: How many people shared the paratha?
qa.a: Four people: Hrithik, Ishita, Papa and Mummy.

qa.q: What might Hrithik have felt when he worked out that two quarters make a half?
qa.a: He likely felt confident and pleased to finally understand fractions.

qa.q: How could Ishita support Hrithik's new understanding?
qa.a: Ishita could make more everyday fraction puzzles with food or paper for him to solve.

qa.q: How does Ishita see her brother's change?
qa.a: Ishita sees he has improved since last month, though she can't be sure what he was thinking.

grounding: An older sister watches her brother grasp quarters and halves by sharing a paratha.

passage:
First week: Santosh, eight, counted on his fingers to do 15 minus 7 and kept losing track. His cousin Suraj drew a number line on the back of an envelope.
Two weeks later: Santosh jumped back seven on the line, then said, "Or take away five, then two more." He checked with his fingers and grinned.
A month later: Suraj and Santosh were sharing out 24 marbles among four friends. Santosh said, "Six each," before Suraj finished counting. "How?" "Four sixes are twenty-four. Easy!" Suraj nodded, impressed.

qa.q: What did Suraj draw the number line on?
qa.a: The back of an envelope.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when he grinned after checking with his fingers?
qa.a: He felt pleased and confident that his new method gave the right answer.

qa.q: What helped Santosh move beyond counting on his fingers?
qa.a: Suraj gave him a number line, which let him see jumps and break numbers into easier parts.

qa.q: How does Suraj see Santosh's progress by the end?
qa.a: Suraj is impressed that Santosh can now divide marbles quickly using multiplication.

grounding: Over a month, a boy moves from finger-counting to using number lines and multiplication.

passage:
Come, Lavanya, bring your maths book. Your Shankar Thatha will tell you how I learned fractions. Not from a book.

When I was nine, our village had a jackfruit tree. One day Amma cut a jackfruit and said, "Shankar, share it equally among you four." There were four of us, and one big jackfruit.

I wanted the biggest piece, of course. But my younger sister was watching. So I cut it in half, then each half in half again. Four pieces. "Each one is a quarter," Amma said. That was the first time I heard the word.

Then my cousin came. Five people! I had to cut again. Everybody got a smaller piece. I learned that day: more people, smaller share.

So, Lavanya, don't just learn fractions. Cut a jackfruit.

qa.q: How many children were there before the cousin came?
qa.a: There were four of them.

qa.q: How might young Shankar have felt when the cousin arrived?
qa.a: Young Shankar was probably a bit disappointed, since everyone's share got smaller.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help Shankar learn?
qa.a: Cutting the jackfruit in half and half again made the idea of quarters real, and re-cutting for five showed that more people means smaller shares.

qa.q: How might Shankar's younger sister have felt watching him cut the fruit?
qa.a: She was likely hopeful and watchful, wanting a fair share.

grounding: A grandfather tells how, at nine, he learned fractions by sharing a jackfruit equally among siblings.

passage:
The Diwali stall outside the family shop in Indore was crowded, and Papa was busy with the big customers. Aparna, nine, and her brother Tarun, seven, ran the small table of diyas.

"Four packets," said a lady. "How much?"

Each packet cost fifteen rupees. Aparna counted on her fingers: fifteen, thirty, forty-five, sixty. "Sixty rupees."

The lady gave her a hundred-rupee note. Aparna thought fast. "A hundred minus sixty... forty." She gave back forty.

Tarun stared. "How did you do that so fast?"

"Four fifteens is sixty," Aparna said. "I'll teach you tomorrow."

qa.q: How much did each packet cost?
qa.a: Each packet cost fifteen rupees.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel when Tarun asked how she did it so fast?
qa.a: Aparna felt proud and confident about her maths skills.

qa.q: How could Papa help Aparna build on her arithmetic?
qa.a: He could let her keep helping at the stall and ask her to explain her method to Tarun.

qa.q: How might the customer feel getting the right change quickly?
qa.a: The customer was likely impressed and satisfied.

grounding: On a busy Diwali stall, a child uses multiplication and subtraction to work out prices and change.

passage:
It was a hot May afternoon in the summer holidays in Chennai. Usha, ten, and her friend Rashmi had one big dosa between them and Usha's little brother.

"Three people," Usha said. "So each of us gets a third."

Rashmi frowned. "But your brother is small. Can he have less?"

"Then it's not equal," Usha said. "If we cut it in thirds, it's fair."

She folded the dosa and cut it carefully. "One, two, three. One third each."

Her brother grabbed his. "Mine is the biggest!"

"No, they're all the same," Usha laughed. "That's what thirds means."

qa.q: How many people shared the dosa?
qa.a: Three people shared it.

qa.q: How did Usha feel when her brother said his was the biggest?
qa.a: Usha felt amused, laughing and explaining that the pieces were the same.

qa.q: How did Usha use fractions in a fair way?
qa.a: She divided the dosa into three equal parts, one third each, so everyone got the same.

qa.q: How might Rashmi see the idea of cutting it into thirds?
qa.a: Rashmi first thought the small brother could have less, but likely understood the fairness after Usha explained.

grounding: On a summer afternoon, a child uses fractions to share a dosa equally among three people.

passage:
"Damini, there are twelve kaju barfis and four of us. How many does each get?" Tarun asked, holding the Diwali box.
"I'll count them out. One for you, one for me, one for Ma, one for Papa..."
"That's slow. Do it in your head."
"Twelve divided by four... three! Three each."
"Right. Now Ma says she only wants half of hers, and we can share the rest."
Damini frowned. "Half of three is one and a half. So one and a half left over, split between two of us..."
She counted on her fingers, then grinned. "We each get three and three-quarters!"
Tarun blinked. "I hadn't even worked that out yet."

qa.q: How many kaju barfis were in the Diwali box?
qa.a: There were twelve kaju barfis.

qa.q: How might Damini feel when Tarun says the answer hadn't been worked out yet?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and pleased that her fraction answer came first. 😊

qa.q: How could a parent build on Damini's sweet-box maths?
qa.a: They could use more real-life sharing, like cutting a roti into quarters, and let her explain her steps.

qa.q: What is it like for Tarun when Damini solves it first?
qa.a: Tarun is surprised and probably impressed, having set the puzzle without finishing it.

grounding: Shows a child moving beyond counting to division and fractions while sharing festival sweets.
